content: Cutaneous horns, also referred to by their Latin name cornu cutaneum, are rare keratinous skin growths that resemble horns, wood, or coral in appearance. Clinically, they are defined as conical projections that extend above the surface of the skin. While these growths are typically small and localized, there are rare instances where they can grow to a much larger size. Although many cutaneous horns are benign, some can be malignant or premalignant in nature. The exact cause of cutaneous horns remains unknown. This is supported by the observation that these lesions are more commonly found on sun-exposed areas of the body, such as the face and hands. Additionally, there have been reports of cutaneous horns developing from burn scars. A potential association with the human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly the HPV-2 subtype, has also been suggested, as is the case with other wart-like skin conditions. Several notable cases of cutaneous horns have been documented. For example, Zhang Ruifang, a 101-year-old woman from Linlou Village in Henan Province, China, developed a cutaneous horn on her forehead that grew to a length of 6 centimeters. Another horn appeared on the opposite side of her forehead. Similarly, Huang Yuanfan, an 84-year-old man from Ziyuan, China, also developed a cutaneous horn. A historical case involves Madame Dimanche, also known as Widow Sunday, a French woman from the early 19th century. At the age of 76, she grew a horn measuring 24.9 centimeters (9.8 inches) over a period of six years. This horn was successfully removed by the French surgeon Dr. Joseph Souberbeille, and a wax model of her head is now displayed at the Mütter Museum in Philadelphia, USA. In terms of mortality and morbidity, the base of the keratinous lesion is benign in the majority of cases. However, malignancy is observed in up to 20% of cases, with squamous cell carcinoma being the most frequently associated malignancy. The risk of squamous cell carcinoma increases to 37% when the cutaneous horn is located on the penis. Tenderness at the base of the lesion is often an important clinical indicator of a potential underlying squamous cell carcinoma. The diagnosis of a cutaneous horn is primarily made through physical examination. The lesion is visually identified as a keratinous projection extending from the skin. Images and descriptions of cutaneous horns are often included in dermatology atlases to aid in recognition. Treatment of cutaneous horns typically involves the removal of the keratinous growth, which is composed of the same material as fingernails. This can usually be achieved using a sterile razor. However, addressing the underlying condition that caused the horn is crucial. Treatment options may include surgical excision, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy, depending on the nature of the underlying lesion and whether malignancy is present.
